hints: Think about why an M+1 peak appears at all, which isotope of carbon is responsible and what its natural abundance of about 1.1% means.
Set up the ratio calculation as (height of M+1 / height of M) x 100 divided by 1.1 to find the number of carbons.
walkthrough:
Remember where M+1 comes from**
You are looking at a mass spectrum with M at $m/e = 90$ and a small M+1 peak. That small peak is almost entirely due to molecules containing one $^{13}\text{C}$ atom instead of all $^{12}\text{C}$. Since $^{13}\text{C}$ has about 1.1% abundance, each carbon atom contributes about 1.1% to the size of M+1 relative to M.

Do the ratio maths**
First find the percentage size: $$\frac{\text{M+1}}{\text{M}} \times 100 = \frac{0.7}{22.1} \times 100 = 3.17\%$$ Then divide by the contribution per carbon: $$n(\text{C}) = \frac{3.17}{1.1} = 2.88$$ You cannot have 2.88 atoms, so round to the nearest whole number, 3 carbon atoms.

Final answer: number of C = $\frac{0.7}{22.1} \times \frac{100}{1.1} = 2.88 \approx 3$
3 carbon atoms

hints: Start from $M_r = 90$ and subtract the mass of 3 carbons to see what mass is left for H and O.
walkthrough:
Fit H and O to the remaining mass**
Three carbons account for $3 \times 12 = 36$. That leaves $90 - 36 = 54$ for H and O combined. With only C, H and O present, try $\text{O}_{3}$ which is $3 \times 16 = 48$, leaving $54 - 48 = 6$ for hydrogen. That gives $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$ with $M_r = 36 + 6 + 48 = 90$, which fits perfectly.

hints: Recall which bonds absorb above $3000 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and how a free alcohol O-H looks different from a hydrogen bonded acid O-H.
Recall where a strong carbonyl $\text{C=O}$ stretch appears and which functional group must combine $\text{C=O}$ with a very broad $\text{O-H}$.
walkthrough:
Sort the O-H regions**
Both 3350 and 2680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ are in $\text{O-H}$ stretching territory, so the bond type is $\text{O-H}$ in both cases. The key is the shape. A broad strong peak around 3350 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is classic for an alcohol $\text{R-OH}$. A very broad strong peak centred much lower, around 2680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, is diagnostic for the strongly hydrogen bonded $\text{O-H}$ of a carboxylic acid $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.

Add the carbonyl evidence**
The strong sharp peak at 1725 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ is in the carbonyl region, so the bond type is $\text{C=O}$. A $\text{C=O}$ plus the very broad $\text{O-H}$ together point to the same group, a carboxylic acid. So F contains both an alcohol and a carboxylic acid function.

Final answer: 3350 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ broad strong: type $\text{O-H}$, group alcohol
2680 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ very broad strong: type $\text{O-H}$, group carboxylic acid
1725 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ strong: type $\text{C=O}$, group carboxylic acid

hints: Use the total H count of 6 from $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$ to help split the integration, the largest peak must account for 3 H.
Match low shift near 1.4 ppm to alkyl $\text{CH}$ and shifted 3.9 ppm to $\text{CH}$ attached to electronegative oxygen.
Remember that $\text{O-H}$ protons appear as singlets with no splitting and often at distinctive high or mid shifts.
Link the very high shift near 12.9 ppm to the highly deshielded acid proton identified in the IR.
walkthrough:
Use integration to count protons**
From (a)(ii) you have 6 H in total. The peak at 1.4 ppm is clearly the tallest, about three times the others. So assign relative areas 3:1:1:1 which sums to 6. That immediately tells you the 1.4 ppm signal is a $\text{CH}_{3}$ group.

Assign the carbon bound protons**
At $\delta$ 1.4, alkyl $\text{CH}_{3}$ next to $\text{CH}$ is exactly what the Data Booklet predicts. At $\delta$ 3.9, the proton is much more deshielded. That shift means the $\text{CH}$ is attached directly to an electronegative oxygen atom, so $\text{-OCH}$, here $\text{CH-OH}$.

Assign the two O-H protons**
The signals at 4.7 and 12.9 ppm both have area 1 and appear as singlets. $\text{O-H}$ protons do not split. The 4.7 ppm value fits an alcohol $\text{-OH}$, while the very large 12.9 ppm value is characteristic of a carboxylic acid $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ proton, deshielded by two oxygens.

Final answer: 1.4 ppm: $\text{-CH}_{3}$ / alkyl, area 3
3.9 ppm: $\text{-OCH}$ / $\text{CH}$ next to O, area 1
4.7 ppm: $\text{-OH}$ alcohol, area 1
12.9 ppm: $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ carboxylic acid $\text{OH}$, area 1

hints: Look at the shape of the 1.4 ppm signal in the spectrum and count the lines, then apply the n+1 rule in reverse.
walkthrough:
Read the splitting with n+1**
Zoom in on $\delta$ 1.4 in the spectrum. It shows two lines, a doublet. By the n+1 rule, number of peaks = n+1 where n is the number of equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon. A doublet means n = 1, so there is one proton on the neighbouring carbon, the $\text{CH}$ at 3.9 ppm.
Final answer: doublet, due to 1 H on adjacent / neighbouring carbon

hints: Think about which protons are acidic and exchangeable and can swap with deuterium so they disappear from the proton NMR.
walkthrough:
Spot the exchangeable protons**
When shaken with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$, any $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ proton exchanges to $\text{O-D}$ and no longer gives a $^{1}\text{H}$ signal. Here that is the alcohol $\text{OH}$ at 4.7 ppm and the acid $\text{OH}$ at 12.9 ppm. The $\text{C-H}$ signals at 1.4 and 3.9 ppm remain.
Final answer: absorptions at 4.7 and 12.9 ppm ($\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-CO}_{2}\text{H}$) are absent

hints: Join the fragments $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH(O)}$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ into a single chain with only single C-C bonds that fits $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$.
walkthrough:
Build the only fitting skeleton**
You have $\text{CH}_{3}-$ coupled to $-\text{CH}-$, that $\text{CH}$ is bonded to O, plus an alcohol $\text{OH}$ and a $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$. Putting them together with all C-C single bonds gives $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{C(=O)OH}$, which is 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, commonly called lactic acid.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CO}_{2}\text{H}$, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid

hints: Draw a seven membered ring and place two $\text{C=C}$ double bonds in two different relative positions to make P and Q distinct.
walkthrough:
Place the two double bonds differently**
Draw two heptagons in skeletal form. For one isomer put the double bonds conjugated with one single bond between them, cyclohepta-1,3-diene. For the other put them separated by two single bonds, cyclohepta-1,4-diene. Both have formula $\text{C}_{7}\text{H}_{10}$ and are positional isomers of the diene.
Final answer: P = cyclohepta-1,3-diene and Q = cyclohepta-1,4-diene (or vice versa), both shown as seven-membered skeletal rings with two $\text{C=C}$ bonds in different positions

hints: For each diene isomer look for a plane of symmetry through the ring and pair up equivalent carbons.
Count how many unique carbon environments remain after pairing, remembering $\text{C=C}$ carbons are different from $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbons.
walkthrough:
Count environments in P**
In cyclohepta-1,3-diene the symmetry plane cuts through one $\text{CH}_{2}$ and the middle of the opposite bond. This pairs up the carbons to give 4 distinct environments: two different alkene $\text{C}$ types and two different alkane $\text{CH}_{2}$ types. So 4 peaks in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR.

Count environments in Q**
In cyclohepta-1,4-diene a similar symmetry plane pairs carbons to also give 4 distinct environments. Hence Q also shows 4 peaks. Symmetry reduces the 7 carbons to 4 signals in each case.

Final answer: P: 4 peaks
Q: 4 peaks
